title: Trust in protection
hook: he writes that no one can harm the one the Lord protects (Zafarnama)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the coiled one remains: four sons lost, and still something stands. Your line was still standing.

Who gets to say the word safe? A child in a warm house says it easily. A man who, tradition says, has lost his home and his four sons has every reason never to say it again. And yet in the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh writes confident lines about exactly that: being protected. He writes them to the emperor himself, whose armies had chased him. Not a promise of safety from someone who has never been hurt, but from someone who has.
screen: `WHO GETS TO SAY SAFE?` → `WRITTEN AFTER EVERYTHING WAS LOST.` → `SENT TO THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Paraphrased, the thought runs like this: what can an enemy do, when the Friend is kind? The One who protects is the Lord, and no one can harm the one the Lord protects. In the letter, the Friend is God. It can't mean nothing bad will ever happen. The man writing it has already lived through the worst. So protected must mean something else. Some readers hear it this way: what the emperor can reach is the body, the fort, the family's lives. What he cannot reach is the bond between the Guru and God, and the faith that made the Khalsa. That's what is held, and that's what no army can take. The trust doesn't make him passive, either. The same letter argues, accuses, and keeps going. Trust in protection, in the Guru's life, sits right alongside action. It's the floor he stands on while he works, not a reason to stop working. And there's a turn in who he's speaking to. Telling the emperor, in effect, you cannot harm me is not a boast about armies. It's a statement about where real power lies. For the Guru, it lies with the Friend. Sikh prayer, too, asks Waheguru for protection. Read beside this letter, that prayer isn't asking for a life without loss. It's asking to be held through it.
screen: `WHAT CAN AN ENEMY DO?` · `NOT: NOTHING BAD WILL HAPPEN.` · `TRUST SITS RIGHT BESIDE ACTION.` · `WHERE REAL POWER LIES.` · then, large: `PROTECTED.`

segments.voice: Let your weight sink into whatever is holding you up, the chair, the floor, the bed, and notice you didn't have to earn its support. Bring to mind one worry, don't solve it, set it down beside you where you can still see it, and let yourself be held. If you pray, breathe the name Waheguru; if not, rest in the breath itself.
Trust in protection. In the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh writes that no enemy can harm the one the Lord protects, after he had already lost almost everything. Today's word.
Your line: protected. Trust is the floor to stand on while you work. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite prayers for protection in the evening, and the Zafarnama's lines on the Lord as protector are recalled in katha as a picture of trust that stands alongside action.

chat.says: If God protected the Guru, why did he lose so much? Doesn't that disprove it?
options: Not for him. Protection meant what no army could reach: his bond with God and his faith.
It does. The letter admits God stopped protecting him once his sons had died.
Not for him. He meant his army was protected, since it never lost a fight.
chat.meaning: The writer had already lived through the worst, so protected can't mean nothing bad happens. Some readers hear: the emperor could reach the body, not the bond with God.
